title: The Margin
intro: £142 profit. Good? Bad? Right now you can't tell. By the end of this meeting you can.

blocks.html:
Last meeting Grace & Co. made £142 in a week.

Here is the analyst's problem.

£142 is a brilliant week for a lemonade stall.

£142 is a disaster for an airline.

A profit on its own tells you almost nothing.

You have to compare it to something.

blocks.prompt: Start easy. It costs you £20 to make the lemonade. You sell the lot for £30.

blocks.button: The number that judges a profit ✨
blocks.html:
You spent £20.

You made £10 on top of it.

Now compare the profit to what it cost you.

£10 out of £20 is a half.

A half is 50%.

That is your margin.

Margin = profit ÷ cost, as a %

The pounds tell you how much.

The margin tells you how good.

blocks.prompt:
Two market stalls.

The first stall spends £50 and makes £5 of profit. The second stall spends £40 and makes £20 of profit.
 What it costProfit
First stall£50£5
Second stall£40£20
Work out the margin for each one.
blocks.hint: Compare the profit to the cost. £5 out of £50 — what fraction is that? Then turn the fraction into a %.

parts.label: First stall's margin (%)
parts._working: £5 out of £50 = 5/50 = 1/10 = 10%. (Her 10% gear from Unit 1: 10% of £50 is £5 ✓.) The accept list carries 0.1 as well as 10, because the engine reads a typed "10%" as 0.1 — without the twin, a correct answer with a % sign would be marked wrong.

parts.label: Second stall's margin (%)
parts._working: £20 out of £40 = 20/40 = 1/2 = 50%. Decimal twin 0.5 included for the same reason as part a.

blocks.prompt:
The board meeting that matters.

Ana spends £100 and makes £20 of profit.

Ben spends £400 and also makes £20 of profit.
 What they spendProfit
Ana£100£20
Ben£400£20
They made the same profit. Are they the same business?
blocks.hint: Work out each margin. Ana: £20 out of £100. Ben: £20 out of £400.

parts.label: Ana's margin (%)
parts._working: 20/100 = 20%. (20 out of 100 is the easiest percentage there is — out of 100 means it IS the percentage.)

parts.label: Better business? (Ana or Ben)
parts._working: Ana. Same £20 of profit out of a quarter of the money. Text parts mark as "review" rather than wrong if they miss, but in practice mode a miss still shows "try again" — hence the spelling variants.

blocks.button: Why the margin is the judge ✨
blocks.html:
Both of them made £20.

Ana risked £100 to get it.

Ben had to find £400 for the same £20.

Ben probably borrowed most of that.

Borrowing costs money. And lenders get nervous.

The margin tells you how hard your money is working.

20% is money working hard.

5% is money working slowly — and Ben has four times as much of it stuck in the business.

blocks.prompt: Now run it forwards. You want a 50% margin. A crate of lemons costs you £30.
blocks.hint: First: 50% of £30 is the profit you need. Then add that profit onto the cost to get your price.

parts.label: So you must sell for (£)
parts._working: Cost + profit = 30 + 15 = £45. Check the margin back: profit 15 out of cost 30 = 1/2 = 50% ✓.

blocks.prompt:
Boss question — and a rematch. The profit-as-a-percentage question got away from you on the diagnostic. It comes back now that you have the margin.

You buy a box of trainers for £80. You sell them for £100.
blocks.hint: Profit first: £100 − £80. Then compare that profit to the £80 it cost you. Your quarter gear will help.

parts.label: Margin (%)
parts._working: £20 out of £80 = 20/80 = 1/4 = 25%. Gear check from w1s2: a quarter of £80 is £20 ✓. Decimal twin 0.25 included so a typed "25%" also marks correct.

blocks.prompt:
★ The analyst's trap. Two businesses, one afternoon.

Business A spends £40, and its margin is 50%.

Business B spends £200, and its margin is 20%.
 What it spendsMargin
Business A£4050%
Business B£20020%
Which one puts more money in the till?
blocks.hint: Turn each margin back into pounds. 50% of £40. Then 20% of £200.

parts.label: More money? (A or B)
parts._working: B. Half the margin, twice the money — because B is working with five times as much cost. The margin judges a profit; it does not by itself tell you the size of one. This is the guard against over-learning the reveal.

blocks.html:
📈 Market story for the dinner table:

Spend £100 in a supermarket's world and it gets back about £103.

Spend £100 in a luxury handbag shop's world and it gets back about £170.

The supermarket is worth far more money than the handbag shop.

Board question for Dad: how can the tiny-margin business beat the huge-margin one?

(Your ★ question is the clue. Think about how many times a supermarket spends and gets its money back in a single day — and how many handbags that shop sells before lunchtime.)

Then the analyst's own question: which of the two would you rather own, and why?

done.title: Meeting adjourned ✓
done.html:
The margin: the number that judges a profit.

You can find it, you can run it backwards to set a price, and you know its trap — a big margin on a small business can lose to a small margin on a big one.
